title: Save the burning world
hookLine: the world is burning; save it by whatever door it can be saved (Bilaval Var M3, ang 853)

cards: A house is on fire. Smoke at the windows, people inside. Nobody on the lawn holds a meeting about which door is the proper one.
Front door, back door, a ladder at the upstairs window: whichever opening gets someone out is the right one. Guru Amar Das, who spoke to the single mind, now pulls the camera all the way back.
In a salok in the Var of Raga Bilaval, he looks at the whole world, sees it burning, and asks for it to be saved by any door at all.

teach.b: The salok, paraphrased: the world is burning; save it, Lord, by Your mercy. By whatever door it can be rescued, rescue it that way.
It goes on: the True Guru shows the way of peace, through reflecting on the true Word, and Nanak knows no other who forgives. Three things to slow down for. First, who's being asked.
This is a prayer to God, not a project plan for heroes. The rescuing is in the Lord's hands, and the Guru is the one asking. Second, what's burning.
Some readers hear an inner fire: craving, anger, ego, a world on fire from the inside.
Third, the phrase at the center: jit duarai, by whatever door. The salok doesn't name one entrance and close the others. It asks for mercy through whichever door will work.

teach.h: READ AS GENEROSITY, OR GOD'S FREEDOM.
teach.b: Sikhs read that phrase in more than one way. Some hear a wide generosity: the Guru wants everyone rescued and doesn't haggle over how.
Others hear the Lord's freedom: God knows which door suits each person, and the asking leaves that choice to God. Some hold both. Either way, the prayer is open-handed.
And it leaves a question for whoever says it: is there a door I could open myself? That's today's line.

how: Sikhs hear this salok of Guru Amar Das in kirtan and katha, and some recite its opening lines as a prayer for the world.

games.q: what does “save the burning world” mean?
o: a call for Sikhs to fight the fires of war
a prayer that God save the world by whatever door
a warning that the world will end in flames

games.q: inside the salok: tap the pairs.

s: the salok names one single door through which the world must be saved
it asks for rescue by whatever door the world can be saved.
the salok is addressed to God as a prayer
it asks the Lord, by His mercy, to save the burning world.
the salok says the True Guru shows the way of peace through the true Word
after the plea for the burning world, it says the True Guru shows peace through reflecting on the true Word.

games.q: you see the world burning and you're asking for it to be saved. how do you ask?
o: save it, but only through the proper door.
save it, by whatever door it can be saved.
save the ones who deserve it.
games.why: Guru Amar Das asks for rescue by whatever door works, and leaves the how to God's mercy.

practice: Think of one person who seems to be burning a little right now, stressed, grieving or stuck, and instead of planning a rescue, ask which door is open to you: a message, a meal, a ride, a quiet stretch of listening.
Let one door come clear, and rest there. If you pray, hold them in the salok's words: save them by whatever door they can be saved.

wordCard.voice: Save the burning world. Guru Amar Das's prayer in Raga Bilaval: the world is burning; by Your mercy, save it, by whatever door it can be saved. Today's word.

orig.note: the burning world, in the opening of Guru Amar Das's salok in the Var of Raga Bilaval.

carryVoice: Your line: by any door. Even a small door, opened, counts for something. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Bilaval ki Var, salok Mahala 3, Ang 853 (jagat jalanda rakh lai; jit duarai ubrai titai laihu ubar)
